pending_articles.title: Theta and High-alpha Phase-locking Dynamics Unveil Face Perception in Ambiguous Stimuli
pending_articles.content: Previous studies emphasize phase synchronization as a fundamental mechanism for integrating local features into coherent percepts. We employed a novel paradigm and dynamic graph analysis based on EEG to track neural dynamics associated with perceiving a face (or not) while keeping the stimuli identical. Thirty participants underwent a pretest to establish perceptual thresholds for detecting faces within images overlaid with visual noise. These thresholds were then applied in an EEG experiment with the same task, focusing on images with 50% and 75% detection probabilities. In the high-alpha band, we observed increased coupling (100–275 msec after stimulus onset) between the left and right occipitotemporal electrodes when an ambiguous stimulus was perceived as a face, indicating conscious face perception. The failure to perceive a face resulted in enhanced theta band phase synchronization between bilateral occipitotemporal electrodes and increased high-alpha-band coupling between the left frontal and right occipitotemporal electrodes, which showed face-selective responses. These synchronizations are likely to reflect the continuous gathering of individual bits of facial information rather than signaling the presence or absence of a face percept. Additionally, we identified frontal–occipitotemporal theta-band couplings related to the stimulus’s informational content, irrespective of whether the inherent face was perceived. Our findings reveal distinct temporal dynamics in phase synchronization at specific frequencies, indicating a specialized system for face perception during integrated information processing across the frontal and visual cortex, resolving ambiguities.

pending_articles.title: Capturing the Attentional Trade-off between Speech Planning and Comprehension
pending_articles.content: In conversation, future speakers often plan speech simultaneously with comprehension, which means that they must divide attentional resources between these processes. In this EEG study, we used responses to linguistic attention probes (i.e., syllable “BA” presented during spoken sentences) to track temporal variations in attention to comprehension. Participants were asked to listen to prerecorded sentences with expected or unexpected sentence-final words. Each sentence was presented twice, once with and once without the attention probe starting 100 msec after the target word onset. Participants saw a picture 50 msec before the target word. Depending on the test block (picture naming or button press), participants either named the picture or pressed the space bar, both after an 850-msec delay. The probes elicited a negative potential approximately 100 msec after probe onset (i.e., an attention probe effect) in all probe conditions. Unexpectedly, neither word expectancy nor speech planning influenced the timing or strength of the attention probe effect. This indicates that expectancy of words in Dutch does not affect the allocation of attention toward these words 100 msec after their onset (i.e., the time of the probe presentation). Interestingly, engaging in speech planning does not seem to divert attentional resources away from comprehension at the moment of probe presentation. These findings imply that listeners are able to effectively distribute their attentional resources between comprehension and speech planning and carry out these processes at the same time. Considering these unexpected findings, using attention probes might not be the best approach to capture variations in temporal attention in dual-task paradigms.

pending_articles.title: Gene discovery and pleiotropic architecture of multidimensional pain in a genome-wide association study of >1.2 million individuals
pending_articles.content:
Nature Neuroscience, Published online: 12 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41593-026-02455-1

We conducted a meta-analytic genome-wide association study of multidimensional pain in >1.2 million European-ancestry individuals. We identified 343 independent loci, which, alongside findings from a sex-stratified GWAS and other analyses, expand our knowledge of the genetics of pain.

pending_articles.title: Increased functional connectivity in glioma: separating compensation from tumor-promoting remodeling
pending_articles.content: Increased functional connectivity (FC) in glioma is often interpreted as compensatory neuroplasticity or tumor-promoting circuit remodeling, although FC is a measure of coupling rather than a mechanism. We propose a qualitative framework that first examines whether the measurement is suitable for the claim, then evaluates evidence for patient function and tumor behavior separately. The two lines of evidence are combined only when they concern the same patient context, anatomical compartment, metric, and time course. The framework also distinguishes maladaptive or excitability-related remodeling from tumor promotion. Human longitudinal studies associate network restoration with recovery, whereas experimental cancer neuroscience shows that neural activity and neuron-glioma synapses can promote malignant behavior. Increased FC should therefore be reported with its modality, metric, comparator, compartment, disease phase, reliability, and prespecified outcomes before being interpreted as compensatory, maladaptive, or tumor-promoting.

pending_articles.title: Magnetic susceptibility source separation technology: a narrative review of principles, validation, and clinical translation
pending_articles.content: Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) returns the net susceptibility of each voxel. When paramagnetic and diamagnetic materials coexist, their opposing contributions can cancel, and QSM cannot recover them separately. Magnetic susceptibility source separation (MSSS) adds a relaxation-sensitive measurement, usually R2′ or a calibrated estimate derived from R2*, to the signed local field. The combined data are used to estimate paramagnetic- and diamagnetic-associated components. In this narrative review, we examine the acquisition demands, physical assumptions, validation, and clinical use of the main MSSS methods. We consider R2′-based χ-separation, the GRE-only DECOMPOSE-QSM and R2*QSM methods, adaptive-parameter techniques, and deep-learning pipelines. Simulations and phantom studies support technical feasibility, and a smaller body of ex vivo and in vivo work provides biological and clinical evidence. These maps nevertheless remain model-dependent surrogates, not direct measurements of iron or myelin concentration. Interpretation is affected by susceptibility anisotropy, source geometry, diffusion, multicompartment water, errors in R2 estimation, and differences between scanners and protocols. Early longitudinal studies in multiple sclerosis (MS) have linked component changes to lesion repair. Evidence on paramagnetic rim lesions, however, still comes mainly from conventional phase or QSM imaging, and MSSS-specific clinical data are limited. Studies in Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease are exploratory. Before routine clinical use, MSSS needs real-world validation, anisotropy-aware modeling, harmonized multicenter acquisition, and independent longitudinal testing.

pending_articles.title: Accurate EEG-based linear state-space model of cortical dynamics during a passive motor task with exogenous input
pending_articles.content: Objective. Revealing the dynamics of the brain in the presence of exogenous inputs is crucial for mechanistic understanding, interventions and regulations. We study state-space mathematical modeling of brain’s cortical dynamics using electroencephalography (EEG) data in an experiment with continuous exogenous input. Approach. We use subspace identification techniques to model the brain dynamics in a passive motor task experiment. The EEG data were recorded while participants were seated with their wrist strapped to a haptic manipulator. The manipulator imposed a continuous multisine angular perturbation to the wrist as the exogenous input to the brain. Main result. Using two subspace identification algorithms, we show that linear time-invariant state-space models accurately represent the measurements, in a latent space, assuming that the EEG data are the models’ output. The model is verified and validated using data from seven participants. Moreover, we construct linear maps to relate the latent space dynamics to the neural source space. We verify that the findings of our model align with those identified in previous studies. Significance. Accurate linear model in the presence of exogenous input provides a pathway for designing parsimonious and simple controllers. In addition, it enables development of online monitoring, connectivity analysis and control relevant to neurorehabilitation, motor learning, and brain-computer interfacing.

recently_processed.title: Slow Oscillations Modulate Overnight Brain Changes in Working Memory Function
recently_processed.content: Working memory (WM), the transient storage and manipulation of information, is a cognitive function that can improve with training. Accumulating evidence suggests that sleep, particularly slow oscillations (SOs) that occur during nonrapid eye movement sleep, supports this improvement. Yet, how sleep and SOs in particular relate to neural processes supporting WM remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated how WM-related neural activity evolves across nocturnal sleep and how these changes relate to neural processing during SOs. Participants performed a WM task during fMRI before and after sleep, with simultaneous EEG–fMRI capturing neural activity during the first 2.5 hr of sleep. Our results showed significant overnight changes in WM-related activity, characterized by reduced recruitment of the dorsal precuneus during WM encoding/maintenance phases and frontal regions during the retrieval phase of WM. In addition, sleep increased item-specific reinstatement in a sensory processing region during WM. This pattern of results suggests a combined influence of sleep on enhancing sensory reinstatement while reducing potential top–down control (i.e., reduced parietal and frontal activity). Critically, SO-related activity was directly linked to overnight activity changes: Stronger SO activation in the premotor cortex and ventromedial pFC predicted greater overnight reductions in WM-related activity, and multivoxel analyses in the ventral attention network revealed a parallel relationship. These findings suggest that SOs play a critical role in WM function by facilitating the reorganization of WM-related processing.

recently_processed.title: Transformer Mechanisms Mimic Frontostriatal Gating Operations When Trained on Human Working Memory Tasks
recently_processed.content: Working memory (WM) is thought to rely on sophisticated frontostriatal mechanisms for selective gating, supporting updating and readout of information to and from distinct memory “addresses” (neural populations). According to computational models, capacity limitations in WM arise due to challenges in “role addressability”: learning to correctly bind items in memory to their respective roles and assigning credit to the corresponding gating operations. However, these conclusions are based on particular assumptions about biological neural networks, and it is unclear whether the principles generalize to other architectures. To address this question, we examine whether similar gating mechanisms emerge in Transformer neural network architectures, which have demonstrated success on tasks requiring executive function—the ability to represent, coordinate, and manage multiple subtasks—yet lack intentionally built-in gating mechanisms. We analyze the mechanisms that emerge within Transformers trained on human WM tasks explicitly designed to place demands on gating. We find that the Transformer's attention mechanism develops role-addressable input and output gating, but only when trained on task distributions that benefit from frontostriatal-like gating mechanisms. Moreover, these gating strategies support enhanced generalization and variable binding and increase the models' effective capacity to store and access multiple items in memory, resembling the constraints found in frontostriatal models. These results suggest that gating mechanisms serve a fundamental computational role in managing role addressability and binding and highlight opportunities for future research on computational similarities between modern artificial intelligence architectures and models of the human brain.

recently_processed.title: Visual Perspective Shapes Subjective Experience: Dissociable Parietal Contributions to the Constructive Nature of Memory
recently_processed.content: Subjective features of memory are often treated as secondary to the objective content of remembered events. However, growing evidence suggests that these features actively shape how memories are constructed, experienced, and used. Rather than treating visual perspective as a peripheral correlate of subjectivity, this review positions it as a key mechanism that shapes the memory. Because perspective can be flexibly controlled and reliably measured, it offers a unique window into how retrieval goals interact with mental simulation to produce vivid and emotionally resonant recollections. Drawing on behavioral and neuroimaging research, this review shows that visual perspective determines the spatial framing of memory and the emotional and sensory qualities of recollection. Focusing on the posterior parietal cortex, it outlines distinct roles for the angular gyrus (AG) and the precuneus in supporting perspective-dependent retrieval. The AG contributes to the selection and maintenance of a retrieval perspective, integrating perceptual and conceptual features into a coherent scene. In contrast, the precuneus supports spatial transformation and modulates the vividness, emotional tone, and embodied character of recollection, particularly when individuals recall events from a nondominant or shifted perspective. Together, these findings position visual perspective as a central mechanism in the construction of subjectivity. Understanding how perspective shapes the process of remembering provides insight into how memory supports emotion regulation, mental simulation, and the continuity of the self across time.

recently_processed.title: Memory Traces Reflect How They Were Last Accessed
recently_processed.content: Episodic memories are known to change with each act of retrieval. We hypothesize that accessing semantic knowledge in different ways during episodic retrieval—from unique perceptual features to taxonomic and thematic context—shapes how those memories are subsequently represented during recognition. In this fMRI study, human participants learned novel word–image pairs and underwent re-exposure that required accessing semantic knowledge at one of three different levels: item, category, or theme. Participants then completed a recognition task. Although behavioral memory performance was matched across conditions, neural activity during recognition varied based on prior semantic access history. Recognition patterns could be classified according to prior semantic access in early visual cortex, ventral temporal cortex, and the hippocampus for remembered concepts. A whole-brain searchlight analysis revealed bilateral clusters along the ventral visual stream where semantic access history was decodable. To further characterize how prior semantic access history shaped neural representations during recognition, we tested whether memories accessed at the same semantic level were expressed more similarly or distinctly in the brain. Category-level access increased similarity among items in early visual cortex, whereas item-level access led to more differentiated representations in the visual word form area. Together, these findings show that how we access semantic knowledge during episodic retrieval leaves measurable traces in subsequent neural representations, revealing how semantic–episodic interactions shape memory representations.

recently_processed.title: The Temporal Dynamics of Attentional Allocation during Counterfactual Learning
recently_processed.content: Counterfactual learning, the ability to learn from what could have happened under different circumstances, is a key cognitive mechanism supporting behavioral adaptation. While its neural and computational underpinnings are increasingly understood, the temporal dynamics of attention toward factual and counterfactual outcomes remain poorly characterized. Here, we investigate the biological mechanisms underlying this process using a reinforcement learning task combined with eye-tracking and pupillometry in 36 human participants. Participants completed a two-armed bandit task with full outcome feedback and exhibited a robust confirmation bias, learning more from outcomes that supported their previous choices. Gaze patterns revealed a consistent temporal sequence of fixations from factual to counterfactual outcomes, modulated in opposite directions by the valence of each outcome. Pupil dilation, a proxy for noradrenergic arousal, was influenced by the factual outcome and by the similarity between factual and counterfactual feedback, consistent with increased surprise during disconfirmatory events. These results provide a mechanistic account of how attentional and arousal systems jointly shape outcome evaluation. By integrating behavioral modeling with physiological markers, this work contributes to a broader understanding of the adaptive constraints on decision-making and offers new insight into how organisms evaluate hypothetical alternatives in learning contexts.

recently_processed.title: When neuroscience meets machine learning: a taxonomic scoping review of machine and statistical learning approaches in sub-Saharan Africa
recently_processed.content: In high-resource economies, computational neuroscience research frequently employs machine learning (ML) and statistical learning (SL) techniques. While these methods provide effective ways to analyse multimodal, high-dimensional, and complex data they are underexplored in low resource settings. This taxonomic scoping review uses a systematic methodological approach to synthesise the application of ML and SL techniques in neuroscience research in sub-Saharan Africa. In addition to discussing findings, strengths, limitations, and future prospects, the work classifies current research by neuroscience domains, applications, learning tasks, datasets, tools, and techniques. In order for African researchers to contribute to and benefit from the global computational neuroscience landscape, our review contends that low- and middle-income countries must create and augment context-specific and representative datasets and incorporate appropriate features for model training. Future studies should focus on pragmatic rather than complex modelling, external validation, reproducibility, interpretability, and utilise real-world data to determine clinical utility.

recently_processed.title: Validation of the Hungarian version of the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised in patients with disorders of consciousness
recently_processed.content: ObjectiveOur objective was to validate the Hungarian version of the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R).DesignWe conducted a multicenter study across neurology, intensive care, neuro-rehabilitation, and nursing departments in Hungary. Thirty-one patients (17 males; mean age 49.1 ± 16.1 years) with disorders of consciousness (DOC) following severe acquired brain injury were assessed. Two independent raters reassessed the same patients within a one-week window to evaluate inter-rater and intra-rater reliability. We assessed reliability using weighted Cohen’s Kappa and evaluated concurrent validity using Spearman’s rank correlation.ResultsConcurrent validity with the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was strong across all raters and time points (rho = 0.882–0.934, p < 0.001). Inter-rater reliability for the total score was excellent at initial assessment (wk = 0.977) and remained high at follow-up (wk = 0.977). Diagnostic classification agreement between raters was nearly perfect (wk = 0.936–1.000).ConclusionThe Hungarian CRS-R is a valid and reliable instrument that preserves the robustness of the original version. Its implementation fills a critical gap in national healthcare by providing an evidence-based tool to reduce DOC misdiagnosis rates.
